correctness.rationale: All complete strict profiles for two and three applicants are exhaustively enumerated. Popularity is computed both by direct head-to-head majority tests and by the Abraham-Irving-Kavitha-Mehlhorn characterization; rank-maximality is computed both from lexicographic signatures and an exact steep-base score. The methods agree profile by profile, and the four-agent witness is exhaustively checked over all twenty-four perfect matchings.

evidence: Abraham et al. define popularity, give the strict-list characterization, exhibit a three-applicant no-popular-matching instance with identical preferences, and state that rank-maximal matchings are not necessarily popular.
Irving et al. define the matching signature and rank-maximality as lexicographic signature maximization.
A later reference entry surveys both popular and rank-maximal one-sided matching as standard criteria without stating the small-market containment boundary.
broader_coverage.reasoning: The prior statement that rank-maximal matchings need not be popular implies existence of some counterexample but does not identify the minimum balanced complete strict size or exclude counterexamples at three applicants when popular matchings exist. The new exhaustive lower bound and explicit four-agent witness supply that missing sharp boundary.

value.rationale: Popularity and rank-maximality are canonical one-sided matching criteria with different normative meanings. The smallest market where rank-maximality can conflict with popularity even though popular matchings exist is a natural boundary. The exact \(3\times3\) census and explicit four-agent witness identify that boundary and quantify the complete preceding finite domain.
